articles.title_orig: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times .
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia told the paper their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia and Megaspeed for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the paper: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed said its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: Beijing drills water cannons and drones near disputed South China Sea shoals
articles.title_zh: Beijing drills water cannons and drones near disputed South China Sea shoals
articles.content_orig:
Training off Second Thomas and Sabina shoals tests small boats, surveillance drones and simulated vessel boardings amid ongoing spats
China’s coastguard has carried out an exercise featuring water cannons and drones near two disputed reefs at the centre of its simmering South China Sea contention with the Philippines to prepare for “foreign infringement”, according to state media.
A China Coast Guard flotilla “recently” conducted “comprehensive maritime law-enforcement training” in the waters around Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal, according to state broadcaster CCTV, which did not specify dates.
The official television network stated that the drill had focused on foreign vessels “illegally” entering the waters around the two shoals, while covering surveillance, tracking, maritime traffic control and tactical manoeuvres by small boats.
It also included practising water cannon use, drone operations and optoelectronic evidence collection – a technique that uses optical and electronic sensors to detect and record evidence that may not be visible to the naked eye – according to the report.

articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Withdrawals After Crypto Hackers Steal $6.3 Billion
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Withdrawals After Crypto Hackers Steal $6.3 Billion
articles.content_orig:
Binance said Friday that a security incident had an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, with around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets frozen so far, and pledged to cover all losses.
The company's co-CEO Richard Teng said the exchange would cover all losses from the $6.3 billion hack using its SAFU fund and company funds, with about $3 billion in stolen assets frozen on-chain so far.
The world's largest crypto exchange said an initial investigation suggests "the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions."
Later in the day, Teng said the attack involved a complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions, underscoring that the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual.
He added that there was no evidence of any wallet private key leak.
Binance has temporarily suspended withdrawals while it overhauls its withdrawal security systems and has revoked the affected address authorizations, Teng said.
The exchange is also working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the stolen funds, while deposits remain unaffected.
Binance co-founder Yi He said deposits remained unaffected and continued to operate normally, while the exchange was working on enhancements to its withdrawal service and related address controls. It expects to begin resuming withdrawal services within the next 48 hours.
The exchange said it would cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company funds, adding that customer funds remained safe.
Binance also temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals, revoked the affected address authorization and enlisted law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover funds.
The company said it would publish a technical report, and an updated Proof of Reserves after remediation efforts.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified," Binance said.
The announcement followed moves by several crypto firms, including Circle Internet Group , Tether and Ripple, to freeze funds tied to the hack.
Bitcoin fell more than 4% to $77,994.96 on Friday as the hack weighed on crypto markets. Shares of Circle tumbled about 5% in after-hours trading on Thursday.
"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," a Binance spokesperson said. "Rest assured that user funds are completely safe." Binance also said on X that Binance Alpha trading had been temporarily suspended, and that "the current verified total frozen is $2.54 billion."
Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said Thursday evening in a social media post that the company had frozen more than 800 million in USD Coin associated with the incident. USDT stablecoin issuer Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino also said in on X that his firm had frozen more than 1.5 billion of its stablecoin that may have been related to a potential breach.
Jack McDonald, Ripple's senior vice president of stablecoins, said it was actively freezing affected funds held in RLUSD, its U.S. dollar-backed stablecoin.
Later, Yi He said in a statement that the XRP and RLUSD-tied firm Ripple helped halt the movement of $200 million of funds linked to the possible attack.
But those frozen funds could represent only part of those impacted. Crypto data provider Arkham Intelligence linked nearly $6 billion in digital assets — including bitcoin , ether , solana and various stablecoins — to 55 wallet addresses it has linked to the potential exploit.
Arkham identifies, tracks and flags crypto wallets by analyzing publicly available blockchain data. It also solicits tips from its community members.
Exploits are not uncommon in the crypto space. In 2025, Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to a hack. More recently, Bitget lost more than $350 million worth of digital assets in a cyber theft incident. Over the past several years, bad actors have also drained billions of dollars in crypto from decentralized exchanges.

articles.title_orig: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Amazon's AI build-out just pushed its cash burn to a record: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
The tech megacaps are collectively placing a multitrillion-dollar bet that their infrastructure spending will result in many years of profitable growth. But that's all in the future.
For now, they're reliant on their legacy businesses — whether it's online advertising, business software or e-commerce — to fund their artificial intelligence ambitions.
Earnings this quarter revealed new levels of strain on those core businesses and offered an early test of whether these companies can sustain extended bouts of spending. Meta joined Alphabet and Amazon in reporting negative free cash flow, leaving Microsoft as the lone hyperscaler to remain positive in that realm.
Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, while Amazon's outflows swelled to $42.4 billion and Alphabet's reached $9.07 billion. Microsoft's cash generation declined dramatically for a second straight quarter, this time dropping 27% to $18.63 billion, and the company said it will now turn to the bond market as it continues to ramp up AI infrastructure spending.
Hyperscaler earnings over the past two weeks have coincided with intensifying concerns about the overall health and stability of the broader AI sector . Rising interest rates are making it costlier for companies to raise debt, putting pressure on cash-burning neoclouds that have become critical to the global buildout.
While the tech giants have a cushion not afforded to the neoclouds and other players, investors eventually need the historic rates of spending to convert into massive new revenue streams. Nerves are hitting the stocks this week, with Alphabet suffering its steepest drop ever on Thursday and Amazon sliding in extended trading after its report.
Amazon said growth slowed in both its retail and ad business. Online sales gained 2% year over year, decelerating from 10% a year ago and falling short of analysts' estimates. The midpoint of Amazon's revenue guidance came in lower than the $244.5 billion that analysts were expecting, a particularly   disappointing figure for the quarter that includes the holiday shopping season.
Meanwhile, Amazon expects capital expenditures this year to reach $220 billion, and analysts project that number will top $280 billion next year, according to FactSet, as the company continues to produce negative free cash flow.
At Meta, investors have responded favorably to the company's early success with its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models , which present potential new sources of revenue outside of advertising.
But it will take time for these efforts to significantly impact the company's overall business while it continues spending on data center and computing gear. Capex will reach as high as $145 billion this year, the company says, and analysts see it passing $210 billion in 2027, alongside a deepening cash flow hole.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% after the earnings report last week even though the company beat on revenue. Meta followed its report by announcing on Monday that it's planning to raise a total of $95 billion in stock to support its AI investments.
Alphabet's report concerned investors the most.
The company's core search business saw a third straight quarter of slowing growth and missed analysts' projections, underscoring the challenges it faces with the rise of ChatGPT, Claude and other AI-powered bots and agents. YouTube-related advertising revenue also came in light.
Mark Mahaney, an analyst at Evercore, told CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime" on Wednesday that while Google's strong cloud revenue was "good news" for the company, its decelerating digital advertising business represented "the overwhelming bad news."
Forrester analyst Tracy Woo said in an email that "Alphabet's massive capex investment in infrastructure buildout has been tolerated for now," but the company "is walking a fine line," due to the online ad sales misses.
"Weakness in Search and YouTube revenue performance relative to expectations surfaces growing concern about AI displacement of the company's largest revenue generators," Woo said. "The issue is less the current earnings miss and more the possibility that future AI spending grows faster than the cash generation of the franchises expected to support it."
But not everyone is concerned. Bullish investors say that the tech leaders have long histories of operations, and legacy businesses that are dominant enough to prop them up for the foreseeable future.
Christopher Ballard, a managing director at Check Capital Management, noted that Alphabet's negative free cash flow of $9 billion is tiny relative to the company's overall business. Its operating income topped $40 billion for the quarter.
Unlike AI model companies OpenAI and Anthropic, which are still unprofitable and spending billions of dollars a quarter on infrastructure, Alphabet has a strong balance sheet, Ballard said.
"They're borrowing from the for-now in order to invest in the future," Ballard said. "I think it's OK, and they're doing it in a responsible manner."
Although the hyperscalers didn't provide specific capex projections for next year, they all implied their data center spending spree will continue to grow, even if it means  reporting some uncomfortable metrics.
"Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years, and you can spread the capex over 25 years?" Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Thursday's earnings call. "Yeah, it might be more convenient, but that's not the world that we live in, and that's not the opportunity."

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Qatar pushes for U.S.-Iran deal under shadow of Trump's threats to resume attacks
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Qatar pushes for U.S.-Iran deal under shadow of Trump's threats to resume attacks
articles.content_orig:
A source familiar with the ongoing diplomacy confirmed to CBS News that Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday to convey the latest edits to a draft proposal to end the U.S. war with Iran.
The source said there were indications of progress being made.
A draft was presented by Qatari mediators last Sunday, and a response from Iran is expected by the weekend. The aim of the proposal is to avert a return to U.S. military action against Iran, which President Trump has threatened multiple times in recent weeks.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that two oil tankers had been halted after unspecified "incidents" as they attempted to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has repeatedly warned shippers that using the southern route through the waterway, which has been promoted by the U.S., puts them at risk as the regime deems it an illegal passage.
The tankers had "switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist U.S. military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route," the IRGC statement said.
The IRGC did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran's armed forces said at least four tankers had been forced to stop in the area after hitting sea mines.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Thursday evening that a tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been hit was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Qatari officials returned to Iran on Friday to push for a peace deal between Tehran and Washington, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency , along with Reuters and AFP, reported.
The talks have been coordinated with the U.S., an official told Reuters.
The delegation is led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister and is scheduled to meet with senior Iranian officials, IRNA said, adding that the discussions would focus on bilateral relations between Iran and Qatar, as well as developments in the region.
An official briefed on the latest diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , and that Tehran would not change its stance on the nuclear issue, something Washington wants included in negotiations from the start.
Tehran wants the U.S. to first lift its blockade of Iranian ports and to drop sanctions limiting the country's gas and oil sales.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by President Trump but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
On Thursday, Mr. Trump said a letter from Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei — which was reported by multiple outlets as an attempt to restart peace negotiations — was an outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran has yet to reply to the letter, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.
Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.
Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.
The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations , which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it stopped using the name Operation Epic Fury for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reported.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
A tanker was struck Thursday evening by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center reported, after Iran's navy claimed four ships had struck sea mines in the area.
UKMTO said the ship hit by a projectile was exiting the strait along the southern route, which the U.S. has encouraged international shipping companies to use, when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," UKMTO said.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its military claimed in two separate announcements earlier Thursday that four tankers had struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires.
It was unclear if the ship reported by UKMTO to have been struck by a projectile was one of the four Iran said had hit mines, but the timing of the report from the maritime monitor suggested it could have been a separate incident.
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.

articles.title_orig: Internal documents reveal scramble for funds before around-the-world "forever cruise" was stranded
articles.title_zh: Internal documents reveal scramble for funds before around-the-world "forever cruise" was stranded
articles.content_orig:
When the journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship came to a sudden end earlier this week in Cambodia, giving residents on the ship just hours to disembark, it marked the culmination of several attempts over a period of about three months to save the unique voyage.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, those included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
The voyage of the Odyssey, which is operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It allowed passengers to become residents of the ship by purchasing cabins for several hundred thousand dollars.
However, more than 200 passengers and dozens of crew members became stranded in Cambodia on Tuesday when Villa Vie suddenly suspended operations because of major financial issues .
In early August, the Odyssey was docked in Singapore when Villa Vie warned that the ship was at risk of being detained and the operator said it urgently needed to raise money.
"There's no question that we ran out of money in Singapore," said Darrell Carp, a Villa Vie resident who told CBS News he is out $250,000.
Multiple residents told CBS News they were concerned about giving money directly to the company because they believed the finances were being mismanaged by Villa Vie.
"We never fully understood the level of their debt," Carp said. "They were already behind on their payments on crew, and provisions, and fuel, and things like that."
A source close to the company said that when fuel prices spiked this year after the U.S. attacked Iran , it was a disaster for the company's business model.
After some passengers raised money while the ship was stuck in Singapore, $400,000 was paid to a fuel supplier directly out of one resident's personal checking account so the Odyssey could continue its journey, sources said.
At that time, Villa Vie was in the hole for several million dollars, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were owed to a port agent, fueling companies, food vendors and the crew.
Those internal documents showed that in a town hall on Aug. 4, residents were warned there was a real possibility of halting operations, laying off staff and repatriating the crew.
According to documents reviewed by CBS News, the ship was potentially days away from losing its insurance. It said that it would cut internet service to save money and was paying just enough to keep sailing.
In early August, Villa Vie introduced a so-called VIP "Villa Incentive Program" to help raise emergency funds, according to the documents. The VIP program was only open to current Villa Vie passengers so they could purchase more cabins at a discounted rate.
By Aug. 18, the company posted: "We have the commitment of over 20 cabins on the VIP sales!"
The program was initially an idea by the residents. Instead of just raising funds, it was designed to give passengers an even greater ownership stake in the ship, according to passengers and a source close to the company.
There was urgency to sell the cabins. The last slide of a PowerPoint presentation by Villa Vie on the VIP program read, "Funds are due today."
The VIP program was able to raise enough funds to keep the ship operating, but it continued to struggle, sources said.
A source with knowledge of the VIP program also said cabins aboard the Odyssey were still being sold to Villa Vie residents despite the company operating at a loss at that point.
According to one document, the ship's finances showed that even at full occupancy, it would operate at a $600,000 loss. Average monthly operating costs were $3.1 million, but revenue at 100% occupancy with everyone paying full fees would only have been $2.5 million, the document showed.
A source close to the company disputes the $3.1 million number, and claims that the ship's monthly operating costs were under $1 million.
In August, 139 of 490 cabins were unsold, according to the documents.
When the ship reached Vietnam, crew members allegedly had to buy food from local grocery stores to feed passengers because the company owed money to a food vendor that would no longer deliver food, according to sources familiar with the situation.
According to one source, the ship's hotel director allegedly had to bribe local customs officials in Vietnam in order to get food onto the ship.
Later, in Hong Kong, court records obtained by CBS News showed the ship was detained until the company paid $167,844.48 to a fuel provider.
Villa Vie Founder Mike Petterson, has said skyrocketing fuel costs were what ultimately caused the ship's journey to come to an end.
When asked by CBS News Wednesday if creditors might seize the ship, Petterson told CBS News: "We will likely file for Chapter 11 here any day, right, which will put a stay on that while we go through the restructure process."
A source close to the company said Villa Vie stopped conducting cabin sales externally after Aug. 4, once the ship knew it was essentially out of money and needed to raise funds.
Yet on July 27, just a week before the ship ran out of money, Villa Vie had announced it was in the process of purchasing a second ship, the Legacy, and offered residents who were buying a cabin on the future ship an opportunity to take up immediate residency on the Odyssey.
A source close to the company said it was necessary to buy more ships to scale up for the business model to work.
This story published first on CBS News at 7:03 a.m. on Oct. 30, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.title_zh: Binance Suspends Transactions After It Is Targeted in Biggest-Ever Cyber Heist
articles.content_orig:
The digital currency exchange Binance says it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist Thursday, believed to be the largest ever recorded.
The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds.
The hack originated from a compromised laptop, it said, which allowed “an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.”
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B,” Binance said late Thursday on X .
About $3 billion of crypto assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said.
Binance will “cover all losses” from the hack, it said, adding, “User funds are safe.”
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice,” it said.
Binance is the world’s largest cryptocurrency trading platform by volume, with hundreds of thousands of users who buy, sell and store billions of dollars’ worth of digital currencies on the exchange.
Unlike traditional bank deposits, funds kept in accounts with companies like Binance are not automatically insured against losses, potentially leaving any refunds up to the discretion of individual exchanges.
The previous record for a crypto heist was $1.5 billion that hackers from North Korea stole from Bybit in February 2025.
Binance cautioned that the full value of assets affected by the hack, as well as assets recovered or frozen, could change.
“ This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets,” it said.
As word of the hack spread online Thursday, major cryptocurrencies traded lower. Bitcoin was down about 4.3%, while Ethereum lost 4.6% of its value.
Two major stablecoin issuers, Tether and Circle, said they had identified billions of dollars in assets connected to the hackers and had frozen them.
Tether froze more than $1.567 billion worth of its digital currency, CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X .
Jeremy Allaire, CEO of stablecoin issuer Circle, said the company had also frozen hundreds of millions of dollars of assets and was coordinating with law enforcement.
The massive breach of Binance occurs at a moment when cybersecurity defenses around the world are on high alert about the possibility of novel attacks facilitated by recent advances in artificial intelligence.
Digital currency has been a primary target of hackers for years. In 2025, Coinbase disclosed that thieves had stolen customers’ personal information and tried to extort the company for $20 million . Coinbase refused to pay and offered a bounty for information leading to arrests, instead.
Binance’s founder, Changpeng Zhao, said, “As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
Zhao stepped down as the CEO of Binance in 2023 and pleaded guilty to breaking U.S. anti-money-laundering laws. President Donald Trump later granted him a full pardon .
David Ingram is a tech reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Giant eagles once ruled the skies. They snatched human children, and shaped our evolution
articles.title_zh: Giant eagles once ruled the skies. They snatched human children, and shaped our evolution
articles.content_orig:
After the dinosaur-killing asteroid hit, giant birds became apex predators for tens of millions of years – and humans were among their prey.
A child of our ancient ancestors, just three years old and still teething , wandered through the swaying grass of the South African savannah 2.8 million years ago. The young Australopithecus africanus was not aware it was being watched from above.
Without warning, an enormous raptor dived . It grabbed the infant and killed it.
Warning: Some readers may find details in this story upsetting.
It's not known for sure what kind of bird ate the early human infant, who has become known as the "Taung child". But puncture marks below his or her eye sockets are consistent with those of eagle talons which hunt their prey in this way, often storing some of their kill in a tree and taking the rest back to its nest.
The Stone Age was a perilous time to be alive. Megafauna came to rule the world . Early humans lived alongside mammoths, mastodons, giant sloths, sabre-toothed cats – and huge child-eating birds.
For tens of millions of years, between the fall of the non-avian dinosaurs and the Great Ice Age, the skies were ruled by these giants. Their reign may have shaped the course of human evolution in profound and overlooked ways. Some are thought to have left their mark in legends of child-snatching birds that have lived on in cultures around the world, long after the birds themselves died out.
When the non-avian dinosaurs were wiped off the planet, the sky was blanketed in dust and most plants died out. For the animals, there was little to eat but seeds – but this suited birds just fine.
In the absence of predators , some small surviving ground-dwelling beaked birds were able to evolve into giants.
Some were plant-eaters , such as Australia's Dromornithidae, known as the "demon ducks of doom" – much like modern-day ducks but 100 times bigger and heavier than cows. Some took to the skies to become huge ocean-going predators , such as the largest known flying bird ever to live, the South Carolina Pelagornis sandersi , with its massive 7m (24ft) wingspan .
Others, though, stepped into the roles left vacant by the extinction of top land-based predators like the Tyrannosaurs. Where there's big prey available, even bigger predators evolve.
These were the monstrous birds our ancestors had to contend with.
"As long as primates have been around, there have been raptors," says Scott McGraw, a primatologist at Ohio State University, US. "And raptors have always been preying on primates – including us and our relatives."
Echoes of the ancient conflict between our ancestors and giant birds can be seen in the wild today. When McGraw examined the remains of more than 600 modern-day primates killed by birds of prey , including African crowned eagles, in Ivory Coast's Taï Forest, he discovered a remarkable similarity with the talon marks left on the Taung child's remains.
In a number of skulls, the monkeys had damage to the orbital floor – a bony surface inside the eye socket – "where the eagle had either pecked out the eyes with its beak, or torn them out with a talon", says McGraw.
"One of our reviewers went down to the fossil vault, pulled out the Taung child, and found that the damage was identical."
McGraw believes raptors would have routinely eaten our human ancestors – and that predation by birds may have been one of the most important selective forces in the evolution of primates, the order to which humans belong.
"If we go back now and examine more closely the [human] fossil assemblages that have been collected over the years," he says, "there is a good chance – now that we know what we're looking for – we will find additional raptor damage. If what we're seeing in Taï is any indication, then this is normal."
There's little doubt in the paleoanthropological record that early humans were prey, says James Cole, archaeologist and dean of applied sciences at Brighton University in the UK. "Particularly the earlier hominins, like the baby Australopithecus africanus that was eaten by an eagle."
Cole says our early ancestors were dinner for many predatory species. "We were predated upon for sure."
The need to evade predators – from birds to leopards , hyenas and giant crocodiles – would have been an important evolutionary pressure on our ancestors. Being dinner for giant birds is thought to have shaped both our bodies and minds .
Our ability to stand on two legs , for example, would have made it easier for us to spot predators. Cooperation and altruism , interdependence and mutual protection may also have helped us. Group size became very important, says Cole. "There is safety in numbers."
When it comes to evading predatory birds, the larger the social group, the better, adds McGraw.
Unlike pursuit predators – such as lions or wolves, which actively chase their prey, raptors are often ambush predators. They are stealthy and, in the case of crowned eagles, hide in the trees until the moment is right. This indicates human tendency towards sociality may have been driven by the need to evade predatory birds in particular , so multiple people can keep watch for a surprise attack – known as the "many eyes effect" .
Cole adds that larger group sizes may have also contributed to the emergence of language. "[In a big group], you start to specialise roles. When you have some people doing one job while others are doing something else, that requires coordination. And once [a group] starts to fragment like that, coordination can't just rely on line of sight."
For simple communication like hand gestures to work, people need to be able to see each other, says Cole, but when you have to coordinate beyond line of sight – say to warn of a predator approaching – "that's where language really starts to play a role".
The pressure to avoid death from above may have even kickstarted language evolution, McGraw suggests. Evidence shows most primates use generalised alarms for various predator types, the same call for a lion or a leopard, for example. But with raptors, they respond with specific calls. Such signalling behaviour, McGraw suggests, could be interpreted as a precursor to human language .
The greatest crossover between giant predatory birds and our human ancestors is thought to have been in the Americas.
Early Americans would have crossed paths with teratorns. These were huge carnivorous birds that could swallow their prey whole . Soaring above the land, these condor-like birds boasted 6m (20ft) wingspans, and were both scavengers and predators . These birds were so huge, they could take to the air simply by opening their wings and getting an updraught, says Joanne Cooper, senior curator of the avian anatomical collections at London's Natural History Museum.
Teratorns ruled the skies for around 25 million years , dying out about 10,000 years ago – well after the arrival of the first humans in the Americas. The teratorn may have inspired the Thunderbird legends, says Cooper. In Native American mythology , the Thunderbird has a colossal wingspan, and is believed to control thunder and lightning .
The Aiolornis incredibilis – also known as the incredible teratorn – terrorised southern California and Nevada and had a wingspan of up to 5.5m (18ft). Further north, in Oregon, the Teratornis woodburnensis had a 4m (14ft) wingspan. This monster of the skies lived about 12,000 years ago. Its remains were found alongside those of mammoths, mastodons and ground sloths – as well as early humans .
Half a world away in New Zealand, the Maori legend of Te Hokioi – a huge eagle that snatched children – is thought to have been based on a real species, the enormous extinct Haast's eagle , experts suggest.
Haast's eagle was "essentially a flying tiger", says Cooper. It was roughly twice the weight of an adult harpy eagle , which is amongst the largest living eagles. The Haast's eagle preyed on another giant, but ground-dwelling, bird, the 4m-tall (13ft) moa . The giant

articles.title_orig: Ukrainians Are Fighting Russians Inside Underground Gas Pipes. I Went in One.
articles.title_zh: Ukrainians Are Fighting Russians Inside Underground Gas Pipes. I Went in One.
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian president says Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position strongest ⁠in some ​time. What we know on day 1,708
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukrainian forces are retaking territory through a series of offensives , adding Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position was the strongest it had been ⁠in some ​time. The Ukrainian president, citing ⁠a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in ⁠eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in ​key areas.
The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian president Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine. The call by Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to ⁠influence the diplomatic process after US president Donald ⁠Trump stunned allies by agreeing to buy Russian diesel, plunging ties with Ukraine to their lowest point in 18 months.
While a localised ceasefire appears to holding in Ukraine’s south, Russian strikes damaged a university campus and Kyiv’s important Southern Bridge overnight , in what Zelenskyy described as “a serious escalation” against ​Ukrainian logistics. A Ukrainian military source told Reuters that Russia ‌had hit the bridge with four Iskander ​ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy said energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure in ​10 other regions had also been attacked overnight.
Kyiv plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias ($22 ⁠million) to build water crossings over the River Dnipro that divides ⁠the capital into two ⁠parts , ​the city’s mayor has said, as Russia escalates its attacks on ⁠bridges.
Romanian president Nicusor Dan has called an alleged Russian sabotage plot last month a “grave violation” of the Nato member’s sovereignty and security . Dan’s remarks on Tuesday came a day after the Romanian intelligence service said it identified a Russia-coordinated “sabotage network” linked to a fire in central Brasov County last month, which damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three foreign nationals – two Belarusians and one Ukrainian, all residing in EU countries – were being investigated in connection with the fire. Romania’s foreign ministry said on Tuesday it had summoned Russia’s ambassador in Bucharest. The Russian embassy in Romania said its ambassador rejected the “baseless” accusations.
France has temporarily relocated a maritime patrol aircraft to ⁠Romania to help identify navigation dangers and bolster the protection of critical energy infrastructure ⁠in the Black ⁠Sea. At least eight cargo ships have been hit ⁠near the coast Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, ⁠with about 34 sailors reported dead or missing. Romania’s defence ministry said on Tuesday the purpose is “to identify dangers to navigation and increase the ability to protect critical infrastructure in Romania’s exclusive ⁠economic zone”.
Poland will host a maintenance centre for the US-made Patriot air-defence system. The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the US, deputy defence minister Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on social media. Poland, a Nato member bordering Ukraine, serves as a major logistics hub for military aid sent by Kyiv’s allies. Patriot interceptor missiles are regarded as among Ukraine’s most important air-defence assets as it seeks to repel escalating Russian missile and drone attacks.
Pope Leo XIV’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit the capital, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a ceasefire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during a phone calls with Putin and Zelenskyy.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Third quarter earnings season was in full swing this week, with corporate results dropping from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft ( MSFT ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Amazon ( AMZN ).
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals were represented, as Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Intel ( INTC ), Boeing ( BA ), Ford ( F ), and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) also opened their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data , nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
ExxonMobil ( XOM ) reported third-quarter income that topped expectations on Friday, as the oil major was bolstered by a jump in refining margins triggered by ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
Adjusted earnings per share stood at $4.23 for the period, topping Bloomberg consensus estimates of $4.13.
Twin conflicts — the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine — have disrupted activity at critical fuel-producing facilities, causing prices to spike.
In preliminary earnings earlier this month, ExxonMobil said higher refining margins would add around $4.5 billion to its overall results, following a boost of $4.1 billion in the preceding quarter. The returns echoed similarly solid profits at other Western oil groups, such as Shell and TotalEnergies.
Chevron Corporation ( CVX ) shares are up in premarket trading after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped expectations.
Adjusted earnings were $5.28 per share, surpassing analyst estimates of $4.88, as the energy giant benefited from stronger refining margins and higher crude oil prices. Revenue reached $67.8 billion, exceeding the $60.55 billion consensus estimate and up 36% from $49.7 billion in the same quarter last year.
Chevron stock rose 1% before the bell on Friday.
The company posted adjusted earnings of $10.4 billion for the quarter, compared to $3.6 billion in the prior-year period. U.S. refineries achieved record crude throughput of 1.09 million barrels per day with utilization rates near 98%, while downstream operations delivered significantly higher margins on refined product sales. Shares rose 2.2% following the results.
Reddit ( RDDT ) stock plunged 17% after hours. The company reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings and revenue, but investors were disappointed by softer-than-expected US daily active users and a subdued fourth quarter outlook.
Here's what Reddit reported in the third quarter, compared to analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:
Revenue: up 53% year over year to $895 million, beating estimates of $875 million
Global daily active users (DAUs): increased 12% year over year to 130.3 million
US daily active users: decreased 2% year over year to 50.7 million
International daily active users: i ncreased 24% year over year to 79.6 million
Earnings per share: $1.40, versus $1.33 expected
Q4 revenue guidance: $1 billion to $1.03 billion, lighter than the $1.04 billion forecast by Wall Street
Q4 adjusted EBITDA guidance: $480 million to $510 million, with a midpoint below the $509 million expected
Amazon ( AMZN ) reported third quarter results Thursday, missing on the top and bottom lines, sending the stock falling.
Follow live updates from the report and earnings call here >
Starbucks ( SBUX ) earnings beat expectations on Thursday, as the company looked to move beyond its turnaround plan to accelerate growth.
For the fifth consecutive quarter, the coffee giant posted better-than-expected same-store sales growth, up 7.2%, compared to Wall Street's expectations of 6.2%. That was driven by US sales, which were up 7.7%, with roughly a 5% increase in ticket sizes as customers spent more at Starbucks and roughly a 2% increase in transactions.
"We have a clear plan. We've been working the plan. And the plan is working," CEO Brian Niccol said in prepared remarks. He added that the company is "operating with greater consistency" and that more customers are going to Starbucks.
Adjusted earnings came in at $0.80, more than the $0.71 Wall Street forecast. Revenue fell short, at $9.1 billion, compared with the $9.2 billion the Street was looking for, reflecting the sale of Starbucks China business.
International sales fell short of Wall Street's expectations, rising just 0.9% compared to the roughly 3% growth the Street was looking for.
Intel ( INTC ) reported better-than-anticipated third-quarter earnings after the bell Thursday, but Q4 revenue outlook fell short of Wall Street's expectations on declining PC sales.
Intel stock fell more than 20% on the news.
In the fourth quarter, Intel is projecting revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the $17 billion analysts expected.
Intel says the shortfall is a result of a worse-than-anticipated drop in PC revenue. The industry is contending with two overlapping factors at the moment: difficult comparisons to last year, when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, forcing enterprises around the world to purchase newer Windows 11 systems, and the steady increase in PC prices, which is eating into demand.
Rivian ( RIVN ) reported upbeat third quarter results after the bell on Thursday and boosted its guidance, citing strong R2 sales.
Rivian reported Q3 revenue of $2.155 billion vs. $2.02 billion per Bloomberg consensus, up 38% from a year ago. Rivian posted an adjusted loss per share of $0.48 vs. $0.61, and an adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) loss of $435 million vs. $575.9 million, narrower than the $602 million loss from last year.
Rivian also reported a gross profit of $176 million, up $152 million from a quarter ago, though the automotive segment remained negative.
Rivian stock gained on the news.
Sandisk ( SNDK ) stock climbed in extended trading after solid across-the-board earnings and guidance beats.
Notably, Sandisk announced it will enact an eight-for-one stock split, effective Nov. 19.
Here's what Sandisk reported, compared to analyst estimates compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence:

Earnings per share: $52.60, versus $47.15 expected

Fiscal second quarter adjusted earnings guidance: $55.00 to $57.00 (on a pre-split basis), with a midpoint above the Street's $53.30 forecast
The NAND flash memory maker has been a key beneficiary of the AI data center boom.
"We have started fiscal year 2027 with another quarter of strong performance, with robust and growing demand for our products driving outpaced growth in our data center business," CEO David Goeckeler said in a press release.
The stock has soared in 2026, but it's had a rocky few months as of late. Year to date, shares are up over 460%, but the stock has largely treaded water since July.
Crocs ( CROX ) stock soared 25% on Thursday to its highest price in over two years as investors cheered on a return to growth for the footwear company's HeyDude loafer brand and a brighter outlook for 2026 sales.
In the third quarter, HeyDude revenue increased 6.1% over the previous year to $170 million, marking the first sales increase in six quarters for the struggling shoe brand.

HeyDude makes up roughly 16% of Crocs' total revenue, while the flagship Crocs brand accounts for the remaining 84% of sales.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft's massive employee buyout spooked everyone. Here's what's really going on inside the company.
articles.title_zh: Microsoft's massive employee buyout spooked everyone. Here's what's really going on inside the company.
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft 's huge employee buyout stunned the industry this week, raising urgent questions about why the software giant might want so many people to leave.
Inside the company, concerned staff debated the meaning of the move . Why might Microsoft want to shed 60,000 workers? Will roles be replaced by AI? Are more layoffs ahead?
Business Insider spent recent days speaking with Microsoft insiders to find out what's really happening. The people asked not to be identified discussing sensitive matters.
The main takeaway so far is that Microsoft seems to have unnecessarily spooked employees with the sheer size of its buyout offer, leaving leaders scrambling to calm the troops.
Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood in an internal memo explained the offer was intended to "offer employees agency if they choose to leave the company on their own terms" and said the company expected "very few people" to accept.
Microsoft doubled down later and told Business Insider it anticipates 3,000 or fewer employees will take the buyout. That's only about 5%, or less, of those eligible.
Earlier this year, the company offered a retirement buyout to employees based on age and tenure. About one-third accepted.
Soon after, Microsoft did another round of layoffs . Some employees who didn't accept the retirement offer ended up losing their jobs.
That's led to speculation that more layoffs may come in the wake of this week's bigger buyout offer.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Future workforce needs will continue to be based on business needs and priorities," Microsoft said in a statement.
Business Insider spoke to Microsoft executives who said there are misconceptions about the current buyout offer.
These executives could only speak about their own teams, and they were hesitant to definitively say layoffs aren't coming. However, they pointed out a few differences between the current buyouts and the retirement offer.
"Microsoft doesn't want to shrink by 60,000 people," one executive said, while asking not to be identified. "We are not replacing everyone with AI."
This person thinks Microsoft made latest buyout offer because some employees complained that they weren't eligible for the retirement buyout earlier this year.
And in the case of the retirement buyout, when employees left, Microsoft didn't fill those roles — the headcount went away.
This week's buyout works differently. In some cases, when staff leave this time their roles will be backfilled with new hires.
One reason the latest buyout looks so huge: Some leaders decided it would be simpler to offer it to their entire organization, rather than try to pick which specific teams or individuals should be included.
"It's easier to opt-in giant organizations," one Microsoft executive told Business Insider.
Charles Lamanna, the executive in charge of the Copilot Platform, AI agents, Office and Word, decided to offer it to everyone in his organization, one of the people said. That includes many people in critical positions. The organization is prepared to backfill roles if any of those critical employees accept the buyout, this person said.
Microsoft's key Cloud + AI division took a slightly different approach, according to another executive from the company.
Two teams — Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure and Cloud Operations + Innovation teams — decided not to offer the latest buyout to staff.
Most other groups within the Cloud + AI division did offer the buyout to employees. And this division can backfill some roles, this executive told Business Insider.
Backfilling roles could still help Microsoft cut labor costs. One executive at the company said if a senior person were to leave, they would likely backfill the role with someone more junior who would potentially be paid less. A Microsoft spokesperson said that's not an official company position.
If all this seems overly complex, compared to layoffs, there may be a reason: Microsoft has been under fire for cutting American staff while employing foreign workers.
The Trump administration recently suspended Microsoft from a federal program that sponsors foreign workers for permanent residency, accusing the company of laying off American employees while hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft has denied those claims .
"Never say never, but there's a lot of desire not to do big layoffs, especially as an American company," one of the Microsoft executives told Business Insider.

articles.title_orig: Amazon, Alphabet, SpaceX and Meta are all to blame for the new tech stock rout
articles.title_zh: Amazon, Alphabet, SpaceX and Meta are all to blame for the new tech stock rout
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Don't blame Intel's ( INTC ) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage , for the fresh rout on tech stocks.
Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon ( AMZN ), Alphabet ( GOOGL ) and Meta ( META ) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.
That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.
Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.
Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.
Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.
This compares to a free cash flow inflow of $14.8 billion for the trailing twelve months ended Sept. 30 of last year.
"We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on his earnings call.
Amazon's stock is down 7% in pre-market trading today.
On Wednesday evening, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the quarter versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion.
Thursday saw more than $500 billion in market value wiped off Google.
Meta dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results last week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012. SpaceX ( SPCX ) burned about $9.9 billion in free cash flow in the quarter.
Both stocks have continued to sell off post earnings.
Hyperscaler free cash flow is likely to stay negative points out EvercoreISI strategist Julian Emanuel. The hyperscaler cohort of Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle ( ORCL ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) is now near a negative $200 billion expected over the next year Emanuel's research shows.
This is what the market is pricing in today. Painful, yes.
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

Speaking at an event in New York, he says the relationship is in ‘a more stable place’ but the deep-rooted problems haven’t been solved
A leading economist warned on Thursday that the United States and China are in a “conflicted co-dependency” that this year’s two bilateral summits failed to address.
“You mentioned the two summits that we’ve had this year. Does that address these problems of what I would call a conflicted co-dependency? And you know, my answer is no, not at all.”

articles.title_orig: Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year
articles.title_zh: Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year
articles.content_orig:
Halloween candy is displayed for sale at a Weis Markets grocery store, Thursday, Oct. 22, in Dundalk, Md. Stephanie Scarbrough/AP hide caption
For people stocking up on candy this Halloween, it's a spooky season in the grocery store — and not in a fun way.
Prices for candy, the most popular Halloween purchase, and gum have risen 7.7% in one year and are up more than 18% in two years, according to the latest federal data . That's higher than the average rate of food inflation during that time.
One major culprit: chocolate. Drought and heavy rains in places like West Africa have hurt cocoa harvests in recent seasons and pushed up prices worldwide.
Global cocoa production is now rebounding, but that isn't much help to consumers preparing to hand out candy to peckish trick-or-treaters this weekend, according to David Branch, sector manager with the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.
"The candy on the shelves right now — chocolate candy — that cocoa was purchased in 2025," he said. And last year's cocoa prices were high .
Still, rising consumer prices aren't expected to scare people away from celebrating the holiday, with the National Retail Federation estimating consumers will spend $13.5 billion on Halloween this year. That's a 3% annual increase and sets a record: $115 per person, which is 55 cents more than last year.
There was a surplus in the global supply of beans earlier this year, and cocoa prices have come down from their recent highs..
Yet Branch said consumer chocolate prices are "sticky," meaning they won't fall even when cocoa prices do because of the lag time in production. Manufacturers are also dealing with higher prices on other ingredients like sugar , pricier fuel costs due to the war in Iran and costlier imports subject to U.S. tariffs.
Enna Grazier, who owns the New Hampshire small-batch chocolate company Enna Chocolate, said she is facing a slew of higher costs, including a 50% tariff on some of the holiday packaging and ingredients she planned to purchase from Canadian suppliers.
"I've had to look elsewhere or get creative with some of my packaging needs for this holiday season, and that's super frustrating," Grazier said. "It's meant that I can't plan as far out, or the plans that I did make were disrupted and we've had to pivot and change."
Some candy makers have ushered in a flavor shift in recent years. Companies are offering more gummy and sour candy, and launching products that don't use pricier chocolate, such as KitKat's marshmallow-flavored Witch's Brew and Reese's White Ghosts coated in white creme.
Still, consumer demand for chocolate hasn't melted away. According to data from the market research firm Circana, which tracks purchases in U.S. supermarkets, chocolate candy sales have been increasing for several years running. However, shoppers have been buying less chocolate candy over the same period, which means people are paying more for chocolate and getting less of it.

articles.title_orig: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.title_zh: Chinese Executive Close to Nvidia CEO Suspected of Giving China Information
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China
US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.
Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.
after newsletter promotion
“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

articles.title_orig: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.title_zh: Volkswagen Will Take China-Developed Technology Global In Major Strategy Shift
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen is done keeping its Chinese software locked inside China. The automaker said its China Electronic Architecture (CEA), built with local electric vehicle maker Xpeng , will underpin next-generation models bound for South America and South Africa. That marks a sharp break from the brand's old "in China, for China" approach.
Now that same software stack is being lined up for Europe. A report summarized by Reuters says Volkswagen is studying whether the China Electronic Architecture could form the basis for future mass-market cars from its VW, Skoda, and Cupra brands in Europe, with the plan still under discussion inside the group.
As reported by Reuters , Volkswagen plans to integrate China-developed technology into South American product lineups starting in 2030 . Volkswagen Group China now uses the China Electronic Architecture in five locally produced all-electric Volkswagen brand models, including the Yuzhong 06 and Yuzhong 07.
Volkswagen Group China laid out the broader package, called VEGA, at a Technology Day event in Hefei. VEGA ties together the China Main Platform, the China Electronic Architecture, and China-developed software and driver-assistance systems into one scalable package for software-defined vehicles across multiple segments.
The China Main Platform targets A-segment battery-electric and plug-in-hybrid models. Volkswagen's stated goal is more than 373 miles of CLTC range and roughly 11 kWh per 62 miles in its most efficient version. Volkswagen says the China-built software could extend further still, with the Europe proposal covering roughly three quarters of the next-generation lineups for VW, Skoda, and Cupra .
Exports of China-developed vehicles are also starting to ramp up around 2026. China-built Volkswagens are already heading to markets such as Mexico and parts of Southeast and Central Asia, with more destinations planned afterward. That export push would run alongside the deeper platform integration planned for 2030.
The architecture trims the number of electronic control units by about 30 percent compared with Volkswagen's older setups. Volkswagen says that reduction is central to cutting development costs and complexity across its lineup.
It's a hardware play as much as a software one. Volkswagen intends to bring the same architecture to plug-in-hybrid and combustion models in China by 2027, which would widen its reach past the battery-electric vehicles where it currently lives and give future gas and hybrid products the same software backbone.
Looking further out, Volkswagen is targeting Level 4 automated driving by 2029, built on a third-generation version of the China Electronic Architecture paired with a Volkswagen-developed C7H control chip. That automated-driving target sits alongside the South America plan and the potential European rollout.
The strategy also threatens to sideline Rivian , Volkswagen's US software partner in a $5.8 billion investment central to CEO Oliver Blume's technology plans. A separate report from German outlet Manager Magazin said core brand chief Thomas Schäfer is weighing a proposal to use China-developed software as the basis for future Volkswagen, Skoda, and Cupra models, which would leave Rivian focused on other group brands even if the joint venture itself stays in place.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Hits Russian Oil Refinery, Ending Pause and Defying Trump
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Hits Russian Oil Refinery, Ending Pause and Defying Trump
articles.content_orig:
An oil refinery is on fire in the Russian city of Novokuibyshevsk in Samara Oblast following a drone attack.
Source: Astra , Exilenova+ and other Telegram channels
Details: Telegram channels said that the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery, which produces jet fuel for the Russian forces, is on fire. An air-raid warning had previously been issued in Samara Oblast and the airport had been closed.
Residents of Novokuibyshevsk reported explosions and air defence response on the morning of 30 October. An air-raid warning was officially issued in the oblast at around 06:00, by which time the attack was already underway.
Novokuibyshevsk Oil Refinery has been part of the Rosneft group since 2007. Its annual processing capacity is approximately 8.8 million tonnes of oil.
The refinery produces more than 20-30 types of petroleum products, including Euro 5-standard petrol and diesel fuel, jet fuel for the Russian Aerospace Forces, bitumen and petroleum coke.

articles.title_orig: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.title_zh: Amazon Spending Soars Amid Slowing Growth of Online Business
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent the week punishing Big Tech's biggest AI spenders . Amazon ( AMZN ) just posted the deepest cash burn in its history.
Amazon's free cash flow — the cash left after paying for data centers, warehouses, and equipment — was an outflow of more than $42 billion over the 12 months through September, according to its third quarter results released Thursday. That's nearly double the previous record of about $23 billion, set in 2022 after Amazon overbuilt its warehouse network. Three months earlier, the outflow was less than $8 billion.
One quarter did most of the damage. Amazon spent about $77 billion on property and equipment from July through September, more than double the $35 billion it spent a year earlier. Its operations brought in about $42 billion, leaving a gap of roughly $33 billion over three months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
So far, the spending is working.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) grew 39% to about $46 billion, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon's operating margin of nearly 14% was its highest ever. CEO Andy Jassy said in the release that he projects AWS growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) computing commitments alone amount to about a fifth of AWS's backlog as of June , according to Yahoo Finance calculations based on the AI lab's IPO filing.
Paying for it has meant borrowing. Amazon's long-term debt reached about $173 billion at the end of September, up from about $66 billion at the end of 2025, while its cash fell to about $56 billion from about $87 billion. Meta ( META ) took a different route this week with a nearly $100 billion stock sale .
Bond traders have noticed. The cost of insuring Amazon's debt against default for five years with credit default swaps has risen about 50% since early August, according to Bloomberg data. That price implies roughly a 7% chance of default over five years, up from about 5%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Amazon stock fell about 4% Thursday to its lowest close since July 30 as Alphabet's record drop weighed on Big Tech. It slid further after-hours as sales, earnings, and its profit outlook for the holiday quarter missed estimates.

articles.title_orig: French centrists' feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
articles.title_zh: French centrists' feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
articles.content_orig:
The protests in France have handed Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the country’s far Left, a boost in his presidential campaign.
Polling conducted after the Oct 17 protests shows that Mr Mélenchon has pulled ahead of Édouard Philippe, an ally of Emmanuel Macron, the French president, to become the biggest challenger to Marine Le Pen.
According to the survey, which was conducted for the newspaper Le Parisien, Mr Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, has gained two percentage points since civil unrest peaked in France last weekend, putting him at 17 per cent in the first round compared with an average of 14 per cent for Mr Philippe.
Ms Le Pen, the leader of the hard-Right National Rally, boasts a strong lead , with an average of 33 per cent.
For months, polls predicted that the voting booths would pit Ms Le Pen against Mr Philippe, the leader of the centre-right Horizons party.
But the events of Oct 17, when 550,000 people took part in nationwide protests that spiralled into chaos and looting, have upended the campaign on the Left.
Brice Teinturier, the deputy director general of the polling firm Ipsos, credited Mr Mélenchon’s full-throated support for the student revolt that kicked off last month.
“He has repeatedly emphasised the need to listen to the protesters; that is what has enabled him to rise to prominence,” Mr Teinturier told Le Parisien. “The real protesters have been forgotten by many, but not by him.”
The poll surveyed 1,500 people registered on the electoral lists between Oct 21 and 22.
French students began blockading schools last month to protest against teacher shortages and crumbling schools. Since then, they have been joined by trade unionists and the “yellow vest” movement from 2018, in a convergence of grievances that include the rising cost of living and the erosion of public services.
The protests have driven new momentum for the far Left, and diverted support from Ms Le Pen to her far-Right rival, Éric Zemmour.
Mr Philippe, who served as prime minister for three years under Mr Macron , is losing ground amid fierce anti-government and anti-Macron sentiment. In the best-case scenario, Mr Philippe is projected to secure 15 per cent of the vote in the first round of voting.
“The French believe the government has made poor decisions. Consequently, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, who are part of that government, are being heavily penalised. This trend is accelerating for them,” Mr Teinturier said.
Raphaël Glucksmann, the presidential candidate for the socialists, is also closing the gap with Mr Philippe, with an average of 13 per cent, and has the added advantage of presenting voters with new blood over the old guard.
While the riots were also expected to give Ms Le Pen a boost, the polling shows that they have instead strengthened support for Mr Zemmour, the leader of the ultra-Right-wing Reconquête party, which currently has the support of 4 per cent of voters.
“Marine Le Pen dominates the scene, but she is not capitalising on current events,” Mr Teinturier said.
“She is losing ground as voters are turning back to Zemmour.”
On Sunday, Ms Le Pen launched her presidential campaign in the city of Orleans in front of 8,500 supporters.
Students from the Union of Jewish Students of France infiltrated the rally and heckled Jordan Bardella, the party’s newly re-elected president, during his speech.
Mr Bardella was quick to denounce “this ultra-Left who doesn’t like democracy” and the audience started singing “La Marseillaise” as the protesters were removed.
In her hour-long speech, Ms Le Pen pledged to “restore the rule of law” by automatically and permanently deporting “foreign delinquents” and making rioters pay for damage “their whole life” if they have to.
Without mentioning Ukraine by name, she also said she wanted to make France “a nation of peace” and promised not to send young people to die in “wars that are not ours”.

articles.title_orig: German president confident of resolving trade disagreements with China
articles.title_zh: German president confident of resolving trade disagreements with China
articles.content_orig:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is confident Germany and China can resolve trade disagreements.
A recent agreement on limiting hybrid car exports to the European Union showed that even where things were difficult "there is a way to find solutions," Steinmeier said at the start of his meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing on Friday.
Steinmeier directly addressed the growing imbalance in bilateral trade relations. Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
"We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
When there were problems, Germany would work "to solve them together with you through dialogue," he said.
Steinmeier said China remained important as Germany's largest trading partner and praised the country's "breathtaking pace" in technological and economic development.
Li called Steinmeier a "long-time and good friend" of China.
Germany's president holds a largely ceremonial role but frequently speaks on foreign policy and international affairs.
Steinmeier concludes his nearly week-long visit to China on Friday and is also due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
